text: Your baby is likely reaching for and batting at objects now. Hang a toy within arm's reach and watch them practice their aim.
Your baby may be starting to laugh out loud! These giggles are a wonderful sign of social and emotional development.
Around 3-4 months, your baby may start bringing objects to their mouth. This is how they explore the world, not a sign of hunger.
Your baby can now see colors much better and may show a preference for bold, saturated hues. Try offering brightly colored toys to explore.
Your baby is likely cooing and making vowel-like sounds such as "ooh" and "aah." Respond enthusiastically to encourage more vocalizing — these sounds are the building blocks for later babbling.
Your baby is getting better at holding their head steady and may even push up on their forearms during tummy time. This upper body strength is building toward rolling.
Notice how your baby watches your mouth when you talk? They're studying how sounds are made. Keep talking, singing, and reading to them.
Your baby may be starting to notice cause and effect. Shake a rattle and watch their eyes light up as they begin connecting actions to sounds.
Around this age, your baby may start rolling from tummy to back. Give them plenty of supervised floor time to practice this new skill.
Your baby recognizes familiar faces and may become more animated when they see you, a sibling, or another caregiver. This is secure attachment forming.
Try placing a toy slightly out of reach during tummy time. Your baby may start stretching and pivoting to get it, building core muscles.
Your baby's hand-eye coordination is improving. They may grab at a toy you offer and hold it for several seconds before dropping it.
Blowing raspberries is a new favorite activity for many babies at this age. It's playful but also an important step in learning mouth control for speech.
Your baby may start showing interest in their own reflection. Hold them up to a mirror and enjoy their curiosity!
Babies develop at their own pace. If your baby isn't doing everything listed in milestone charts yet, that's usually fine. Talk to your pediatrician if you have concerns.
Your baby may start bearing some weight on their legs when you hold them in a standing position. This isn't walking practice yet, but it's great strength building.
Watch how your baby studies their own hands, turning them and bringing them together. This hand regard is a fascinating step in body awareness.
Your baby may begin to show different cries or vocalizations for different needs. Responding to these cues teaches them that communication works.
Try holding a toy in front of your baby and see if they reach for it. Reaching with purpose is a wonderful sign of growing hand-eye coordination.
Your baby's vision now extends across the room. They may track people walking by or follow a pet with their eyes. This distance vision is a big leap from the newborn weeks.
If your baby grabs a toy with both hands and brings it to their mouth, they're coordinating multiple muscle groups at once. That's a complex skill in action.
Your baby may start squealing with delight or making high-pitched happy sounds. These expressions of joy show their emotional range is expanding.
Your baby can now follow a moving toy with their eyes from one side to the other. This smooth visual tracking is a big step forward from the jerky eye movements of the newborn weeks.
Your baby is becoming more social and may "talk" to toys, their reflection, or even pictures of faces. Encourage this by joining the conversation.
Try lying your baby on their side during playtime with a toy in front of them. This position encourages the rolling motion and helps them discover new ways to move.
Your baby may experience changes in sleep patterns as their sleep cycles mature. This can temporarily disrupt their sleep, but it's a normal part of development. Hang in there!
Your baby may start consolidating night sleep into longer stretches of 5-6 hours. Celebrate these wins, and know that night wakings are still normal too.
Most babies this age take 3-4 naps a day. Don't worry about a perfect schedule yet — following your baby's sleepy cues is more important.
If your baby is rolling, it's time to stop swaddling. Transition to a sleep sack that leaves arms free so they can move safely.
Wake windows are typically 1.5-2 hours at this age. Putting your baby down before they're overtired makes falling asleep easier.
A consistent pre-sleep routine (e.g., dim lights, book, song, crib) helps signal to your baby that sleep time is coming. Repetition is key.
Short naps of 30-45 minutes are very common at this age as sleep cycles mature. If your baby wakes happy, the nap was likely enough.
If your baby rolls onto their tummy during sleep but can also roll back, it's okay to leave them. Always start them on their back though.
If your baby's sleep is disrupted by a developmental leap, try to be consistent with your approach rather than introducing many new sleep strategies at once.
Daytime naps don't need to be in a pitch-dark room. Some ambient light is fine and helps your baby learn the difference between naps and nighttime sleep.
If you're considering sleep training, most pediatricians recommend waiting until your baby is developmentally ready, which varies for each child. Talk to your doctor about the right timing.
Your baby may start fighting the last nap of the day. This is common — a brief catnap in the late afternoon can help bridge the gap to bedtime.
Try putting your baby down drowsy but awake for at least one nap a day. This gently helps them start learning to fall asleep independently.
An early bedtime between 6:30-8:00 PM often works well at this age. Overtired babies actually have more trouble falling and staying asleep.
Keep the sleep environment cool ({{68-72°F|20-22°C}}). Babies sleep better when they're not too warm.
If your baby wakes exactly 30-45 minutes into a nap, they may be struggling to transition between sleep cycles. Give them a few minutes to see if they resettle on their own.
A sleep sack is a safe alternative to blankets and can become part of your baby's bedtime routine. The act of zipping it up signals that it's sleep time.
If your baby was a great sleeper and suddenly isn't, a developmental sleep regression may be the cause. This is a permanent change in sleep architecture, and they'll adjust.
Try to separate the last feeding of the day from the moment your baby falls asleep. Even a short gap helps reduce the feed-to-sleep association.
Watch for your baby rubbing their eyes, pulling their ears, or getting fussy. These are late sleepy cues, so try to catch them before they're overtired.
If naps are a struggle, try shortening your pre-nap routine to just 5 minutes. A quick wind-down is often enough during the day.
Motion naps in the stroller or car are fine sometimes, but try to offer at least one nap a day in the crib so your baby practices sleeping in a still environment.
Your baby's circadian rhythm is more established now. A consistent wake time in the morning can help anchor the rest of the day's schedule.
If your baby is used to being rocked to sleep, try gradually reducing the rocking over time rather than stopping suddenly. Gentle transitions work best.
Don't compare your baby's sleep to others. Some babies naturally sleep longer stretches earlier, while others take more time. Both are within the range of normal.
Your baby may seem more distractible during feedings, pulling off to look around. Try feeding in a quiet, dimly lit room if this becomes an issue.
Breastfed babies may become more efficient feeders, finishing in 10-15 minutes per side instead of the long sessions from earlier months.
Formula-fed babies typically take about {{4-6 ounces|120-180 ml}} per feeding, 4-6 times a day. But every baby is different — follow their cues.
Even though your baby may seem interested in your food, most pediatric guidelines recommend waiting until around 6 months to start solids in most cases.
Drooling and chewing on hands at this age are usually related to development, not necessarily a sign that your baby needs solid food.

If breastfeeding, you don't need to pump-and-dump after a glass of wine. Experts recommend waiting at least 2 hours after a single drink before nursing, as alcohol leaves breast milk as it leaves your bloodstream.
A growth spurt around 3-4 months may mean extra hungry days. Trust your baby's appetite and feed on demand.
If you're pumping at work, try to pump as often as your baby would feed to maintain supply. Most moms pump every 3-4 hours.
It's normal for breastfed babies to refuse a bottle at first. Try having someone other than the nursing parent offer it, and experiment with different nipple flows.
Your breastfed baby doesn't need water at this age. Breast milk (or formula) provides all the hydration they need, even in hot weather.
If your baby has reflux, keeping them upright for 20-30 minutes after feeding and offering smaller, more frequent feeds can help.
Nipple confusion is less of a concern at this age. If you've been hesitant to introduce a bottle or pacifier, it's generally safe to try now.
Don't add cereal to your baby's bottle. It's a choking risk and doesn't help babies sleep longer despite the common myth.
Continue giving vitamin D drops daily (400 IU) if breastfeeding. Formula-fed babies may not need them if they drink enough fortified formula.
Your baby's feeding patterns may become more predictable, settling into a rough schedule. This makes planning your day a bit easier.
If your breast milk supply seems lower in the afternoon, try power pumping (pump 20 min, rest 10, pump 10, rest 10, pump 10) to boost production.
Your baby may start grabbing at the bottle or breast during feedings. Let them rest their hands on the bottle to encourage early self-feeding skills.
If your baby suddenly wants to nurse more frequently, it doesn't mean your supply is dropping. Growth spurts and comfort nursing are both common right now.
Spit-up often peaks around 3-4 months and gradually decreases. As long as your baby is gaining weight and not in pain, it's usually just a laundry problem.
If you're combo-feeding with both breast milk and formula, that's a perfectly valid approach. Any amount of breast milk has benefits.
Try a slower-flow nipple if your baby gulps, coughs, or seems overwhelmed during bottle feedings. A slower flow lets them control the pace better.
Your baby's total daily intake of breast milk or formula is typically around {{24-32 ounces|710-950 ml}} at this age. Individual feedings may vary, and that's perfectly fine.
Night feedings may naturally decrease as your baby takes in more during the day. Follow their lead rather than forcing a schedule change.
If you notice your baby turning away or pushing the bottle out mid-feeding, respect their cue. They're learning to self-regulate their appetite.
Frozen breast milk may smell or taste slightly different when thawed due to lipase activity. It's still safe and nutritious, even if your baby initially hesitates.
Keeping up with your baby's vaccination schedule protects them during their most vulnerable months. Talk to your pediatrician about which vaccines are due.
Teething can begin as early as 3 months, though teeth usually appear around 6 months. Gum swelling and extra drooling are early signs.
A chilled (not frozen) teething ring or clean wet washcloth can soothe sore gums. Avoid teething gels with benzocaine, which aren't safe for young babies.
Your baby's immune system is getting stronger but still developing. They may catch their first cold around this age, especially if they have older siblings.
For a mild fever after vaccines, extra comfort and fluids are usually all that's needed. Ask your pediatrician about appropriate fever reducers and doses.
Eczema often appears between 2-4 months. Keep skin moisturized with a thick, fragrance-free cream and use gentle, unscented baby products.
Your baby should be tracking objects smoothly and making eye contact by now. If their eyes seem consistently crossed after 3 months, mention it to your doctor.
Apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen to small exposed areas if sun-protective clothing and shade aren't available, even for babies under 6 months.
If your baby has a cough or cold, a cool-mist humidifier in their room and saline nose drops can help them breathe more easily.
Keep track of your baby's growth curve rather than individual measurements. Consistent growth along their own percentile line matters more than the specific number.
Diaper rash is common at this age. Change diapers promptly, let the area air-dry when possible, and use a zinc oxide cream as a barrier.
Babies this age put everything in their mouths. Regularly clean toys and teethers, but there's no need to sterilize everything — some germ exposure is healthy.
Contact your doctor if your baby seems unusually floppy, stiff, or doesn't respond to sounds. Early intervention makes a big difference.
If you notice your baby consistently tilting their head to one side, mention it to your pediatrician. Simple stretching exercises can often correct torticollis.
Your baby may start drooling a lot, which can cause a rash around their chin and neck. Keep the area dry and apply a gentle barrier cream.
If your baby has been scratching at their ears or face, keep their nails trimmed short. Mittens are no longer recommended at this age since they limit hand exploration.
Your baby's immune system is building antibodies with each vaccine dose. Mild side effects like a low-grade fever or fussiness for a day or two are signs their immune system is responding.
If your baby has eczema, try bathing them in lukewarm water for no more than 10 minutes, then apply moisturizer immediately while the skin is still damp.
Flat spots on the back of the head (positional plagiocephaly) are common but usually improve as your baby spends more time upright and in tummy time.
Watch for any signs of hearing difficulty, such as not startling to loud sounds or not turning toward voices. Mention any concerns at your next well visit.
If your baby has a stuffy nose making feeding difficult, try using saline drops and a nasal aspirator a few minutes before mealtime to clear their airways.
Avoid over-the-counter cold medicines for babies under 2 years old. Saline drops, a humidifier, and plenty of fluids are the safest remedies.
Your baby may spit up less as their digestive system matures. If reflux suddenly gets worse rather than better, bring it up with your pediatrician.
Schedule tummy time throughout the day, not just for play but to help relieve gas and aid digestion. Wait at least 20-30 minutes after feeding before placing your baby on their tummy.
If your baby develops a yeast diaper rash (bright red with small satellite spots), it won't respond to regular diaper cream. Ask your pediatrician about an antifungal treatment.
Play peek-a-boo! Your baby loves the surprise of your face appearing and disappearing. This social game builds anticipation and rewards them with connection.
Offer rattles, crinkle toys, and soft blocks for your baby to grasp, shake, and mouth. Different textures and sounds are great for sensory development.
Place your baby on a play mat and let them kick freely. This strengthens leg muscles they'll need for rolling and eventually crawling.
Try "airplane" by lying on your back with your baby on your shins, holding their hands. This builds their core strength and usually gets big laughs.
Blow gentle bubbles near your baby during play time. They'll love tracking the floating movements, which strengthens visual tracking skills.
Hold your baby in a standing position on your lap and let them bounce. They'll love pushing off with their legs and feeling their own strength.
Introduce board books with simple, high-contrast pictures and thick pages. Your baby may try to grab the pages, which is great fine motor practice.
Play "so big!" by stretching your baby's arms up while saying it. Repetitive games like this teach your baby to anticipate and participate.
Take your baby for walks in a stroller or carrier. Point out trees, dogs, cars — everything is new and fascinating to them.
Lay your baby on their back and hold a toy above them to encourage reaching up. This builds arm strength and coordination.
Try making different animal sounds and watch your baby's reaction. Varying your pitch and tone holds their attention and supports listening skills.
Place your baby on a blanket on the grass for outdoor tummy time. The new textures and smells make for rich sensory exploration.
Gently bounce or sway while holding your baby and singing. Movement combined with music is wonderful for their developing vestibular system.
Let your baby play with safe household items like wooden spoons or measuring cups. Sometimes simple objects are more interesting than fancy toys.
Practice assisted sitting by propping your baby up with pillows or holding them in your lap facing outward. This new perspective excites them and builds trunk muscles.
Try a game of "copy cat" where you imitate your baby's sounds and expressions. When they see you mirror them, it encourages more communication.
Introduce a soft ball that your baby can grasp. Rolling it toward them during tummy time encourages them to reach forward and builds arm strength.
Place toys in a circle around your baby during tummy time to encourage pivoting. They'll rotate their body to reach different items, building core muscles.
Let your baby splash gently during bath time. Cause-and-effect play like this is exciting for them and builds hand coordination.
Try playing with a lightweight scarf by letting it drift over your baby. They'll enjoy reaching for it as it floats down, practicing their timing and grasp.
Place your baby in front of a window and let them watch the world outside. Movement, light, and shadows are endlessly interesting at this age.
Offer a toy that makes noise when shaken or squeezed. Your baby is learning that their actions produce results, and this sense of agency thrills them.
Read the same favorite book repeatedly. Babies this age love repetition, and hearing the same words over and over strengthens language pathways in their brain.
Let your baby feel safe objects with different temperatures, like a cool spoon or a warm (not hot) washcloth. Temperature is another rich sensory experience.
Try holding your baby securely and gently tilting them side to side. This vestibular stimulation helps develop balance and is usually met with giggles.
Your baby may start rolling soon, so never leave them unattended on elevated surfaces. Use the safety straps on changing tables.
Check that all toys are too large to fit entirely in your baby's mouth. As they start mouthing everything, choking hazards become a bigger concern.
Your baby's car seat should still be rear-facing. Keep them rear-facing until they reach the maximum height or weight for their seat.
Start babyproofing now, before your baby is mobile. Get down on the floor at baby level and look for hazards you might not notice from standing height.
If your baby is in a bouncer or swing, always use the safety harness and place it on the floor, never on a table or counter.
Secure furniture to the walls with anti-tip brackets. It might seem early, but once your baby is mobile, unsecured furniture is a serious risk.
Cover electrical outlets with safety caps or outlet covers. Your baby will be reaching and grabbing at everything within a few months.
Check your baby's crib: the mattress should fit snugly with no gaps bigger than two fingers between the mattress and the frame.
Keep hot beverages well out of reach when holding your baby. A spilled cup of coffee can cause serious burns to delicate baby skin.
Never shake your baby, even in play. If you're feeling overwhelmed, put your baby in a safe place and step away for a moment to collect yourself.
Set your water heater to {{120°F|49°C}} or below to prevent accidental scalding during bath time.
When using an activity center or floor seat, make sure your baby is developmentally ready (good head control) and limit time to short sessions.
Keep small batteries, especially button batteries, completely out of reach. If swallowed, they can cause severe internal burns within hours.
Consider taking an infant CPR class. Knowing what to do in an emergency gives you confidence and could save your baby's life.
If your baby has started rolling, remove any mobiles or hanging toys from the crib that they might reach, pull down, and become entangled in.
Keep plastic bags, wrapping materials, and packaging away from your baby. These can be suffocation hazards even when your baby seems too young to grab them.
Make sure all caregivers and babysitters know your baby's sleep safety rules: back to sleep, firm flat surface, nothing in the crib.
If your baby can reach the sides of their crib or bassinet while lying down, it may be time to transition to a full-size crib for more room to move safely.
Avoid propping a bottle for your baby to feed unattended. Propped bottles can cause choking, ear infections, and tooth decay.
When wearing your baby in a carrier, avoid cooking, drinking hot liquids, or standing near heat sources. Your baby is closer to hazards than you might realize.
Check the recall list for any baby gear you own or receive secondhand. Older products may not meet current safety standards.
Keep your phone's volume on when your baby is sleeping so you can hear a monitor alert. But resist the urge to check the video at every sound — some noise is normal.
Avoid leaving your baby in a car seat for extended periods outside the car. The semi-reclined angle can restrict breathing, especially in younger infants.
Now that your baby is grabbing at everything, be mindful of dangling jewelry, glasses, and hair when holding them. A strong baby grip can pull surprisingly hard.
Keep cleaning products, laundry pods, and dishwasher tablets in locked cabinets. Their bright colors and squishy textures make them dangerously attractive to babies.
